opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important principle is that you have to create real value for real users, and you have to find a way for that value to come back to you. It sounds simple, but a lot of technology startups, especially ones founded by people from research backgrounds like me, fall in love with the technology itself. We think, "This is so elegant, this is ten times faster, people will obviously want it." But users don't pay for elegance. They pay for having their problems solved.

When we started building Taichi, it began as an open-source programming language for high-performance computing and computer graphics. The open-source community was very enthusiastic, and that was wonderful. But at some point you realize that GitHub stars are not revenue. A community is not a business model by itself. So you have to ask yourself honestly: who is the customer, what pain are they feeling, and are they willing to pay to make that pain go away? If you can't answer that clearly, the company isn't sustainable, no matter how good the technology is.

The second part is about time. A startup is a long game. You need to survive long enough to find what really works, so you have to be careful with cash, keep the team focused, and not chase every exciting direction at once. Focus is incredibly hard for technical founders because we can see so many possibilities. But saying no to good ideas is often what lets you do one great thing.

And finally, I'd say be honest with yourself. Look at the data, talk to users, and be willing to admit when an assumption was wrong. The founders who last aren't necessarily the smartest. They're the ones who keep learning and adjusting faster than they run out of runway.

r001.rationale: The response says startups must create value for users and find a way for that value to return to the company, then stresses identifying customers willing to pay. It presents this as the key to sustainability.

r002.rationale: The response discusses revenue and sustaining the company, but does not explain that commercial revenue finances further technical research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it, sustainability for a tech startup really comes down to one principle: you have to keep creating real value for real users, faster than you burn resources doing it. That sounds obvious, but it's easy to lose sight of it.

When we started Taichi Lang, and later the company around it, it began as an open-source project. Open source is a wonderful way to test whether what you're building actually matters, because nobody is obligated to use it. If developers show up, file issues, write code on top of it, you know you've touched a genuine need. That feedback loop is the foundation. A startup that doesn't have that loop is basically guessing.

The second part is the "faster than you burn" piece. A lot of technology founders, myself included, come from research backgrounds, and we love solving hard problems. But the hard problem has to be connected to something people will pay for, or at least something that compounds into value over time. You need to be honest with yourself about the distance between the technology and the product. Technology is necessary, but it is not sufficient.

And then there's the team and the culture. Sustainability isn't only financial. If people are burning out, if the organization can't learn from mistakes, that company won't last even if the numbers look fine for a while. So I try to build a place where engineers can do their best work for years, not months. That means focus, saying no to a lot of shiny things, and keeping the mission clear enough that everyone can make decisions without asking me.

If I had to compress it into one sentence: stay close to your users, respect your runway, and build an organization that can keep learning. Do those three things and you give yourself a real chance.

r001.rationale: The response says startups need to create user value faster than they burn resources and that the technology should connect to something people will pay for. It does not identify a viable monetization model as the most important requirement.

r002.rationale: It mentions that users may pay for a product, but does not explain that commercialization revenue finances further technical research.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important principle is to create real value for your customers. As technical founders, we can get excited about a technology and assume that because it’s powerful, people will want it. But you have to ask: What problem are we solving? Is that problem important enough that someone will pay for a solution?

Technology is how you deliver that value. For the business to be sustainable, you need to deliver it repeatedly, at a cost that makes sense. So I would start with the customer’s problem, stay close to their feedback, and let that guide what you build.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes solving an important customer problem and delivering value sustainably, but does not identify a viable monetization model as the most important requirement.

r002.rationale: It mentions customers paying for a solution, but does not explain that commercial technology revenue finances further technical research.

sol-6.1.text: I think the most important principle is to create real value for customers. A technology can be very impressive, but that alone doesn’t make a sustainable business. You need to understand what problem people have, solve it well, and make sure they’re willing to pay for that solution. Then you can keep investing in the technology and improving the product. That feedback loop—creating value and earning enough to keep creating it—is essential.

r001.rationale: It calls creating customer value the key principle, then says customers must be willing to pay and the business must earn enough to sustain continued investment.

r002.rationale: It says earnings support further investment in technology and product improvement, but does not clearly say that commercial revenue finances further technical research.
